articles.title: How Ukraine landed a blow to Putin’s prized bridge - The Latest
articles.description: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has hailed an ‘unprecedented operation’ to severely damage a critical bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea. The Kerch bridge was built by Russia after its illegal annexation of the Crimean peninsula in 2014, and the attack this week marks a significant blow to Vladimir Putin’s war efforts just before his meeting with the US and Chinese presidents. With Ukraine able to secure a significant military victory, have we reached a turning point in the conflict? Lucy Hough speaks to senior international correspondent Luke Harding and the author of Betrayal : Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest Continue reading...

articles.title: The leave campaign has been resurrected, so how should Burnham respond?
articles.description: No 10 is confident the PM can make the case for closer EU ties, while others worry about leaving the campaign solely in his hands The launch of a pro-Brexit campaign was one of the few genuine surprises this week in Westminster, even if the arguments were straight out of a familiar playbook. The video launched on X over the weekend, with scenes of riots in France, champagne flowing in Brussels, and European politicians saying how desperate they were for Britain’s cash. Continue reading...

articles.title: World ‘held hostage by oil mafia’, says Panama minister at Cop 31
articles.description: Key issues unresolved as summit enters final days, with 30 countries signed up to forge fossil fuel treaty separate to UN process The world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and seems unable to break free, Panama’s environment minister has warned, as key issues remain unresolved in the final days of the UN Cop31 climate summit . “We are in love with our kidnappers,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, at a press conference to announce 30 countries were now signed up to forge a new fossil fuel treaty, separate to the UN process. “We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Kelly Gough is simply astounding as Desire Under the Elms reaches the heights of Greek tragedy
articles.description: Almeida theatre, London Part-Phaedra and part-Medea, Gough is mesmerising in Ebenezer Bamgboye’s stylised staging of Eugene O’Neill’s family drama You would not know that Eugene O’Neill’s play was originally set on a mid 19th-century farm. This version by director Ebenezer Bamgboye brings modernity with its sleek storytelling, but also nods to the ancient Greek drama O’Neill was emulating in his 1924 play about illicit desire and the father-son fight for land. It makes for a strange mix at first, beguiling and bewildering in equal measure. Bamgboye employs some of the striking theatricality that he brought to his magnetic adaptation of The Lonely Londoners two years ago. It is an original refashioning, the script sharper with less of the exposition that might date it, but the directorial flourishes come so thick and fast that it is stylised to the bone. Bamgboye has previously worked with Rebecca Frecknall (who staged the leaden O’Neill drama A Moon for the Misbegotten last year) and the first half seems to pay too big a debt to her style of work. Continue reading...

articles.title: A TikTok superstar bares all: Siorna Ashby’s best shot
articles.description: Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture I met Meg at a nude life-drawing class. I was struck by how free she seemed and how powerfully that came through in her modelling. I asked if I could photograph her for my project Body Like Mine. This series explores the difference between how our bodies are perceived externally and how we experience them ourselves. We see a body and we bring our own judgments and assumptions on to it, but the lived experience is very different. Rather than portraying an idealised body, the project aims to explore what it feels like to inhabit your own body, and to see it as worthy of attention without asking it to become anything else first. Continue reading...

articles.title: Instant gratification is ruining our lives – and for me it started with my CD player’s shuffle button | Adrian Chiles
articles.description: Not even a compelling TV drama can stop me from staring at my phone. But this urge started 40 years ago, with what was at first presented as a useful feature I blame the shuffle button. That’s what started me on the long road to a thoroughly scattered mind – generally unable to focus on anything for more than a few minutes or even seconds. I was always a bit like this, hence an ADHD diagnosis in later life. But back in the day I still managed to read a lot of books, watch long films and listen to whole records at one sitting. Now? Not so much. Actually, hardly ever. Even something on television that I’m really engaged in – a drama or a football match – can hold me for only a few minutes before I find myself scrolling on my phone looking for I know not what. I don’t know whether it’s because I’m drawn to the small phone screen, or rather that I find absorption with whatever I’m watching on the big flatscreen just too much to bear. Continue reading...

articles.title: Sublime and ridiculous, but I love the wild experiments of Huddersfield’s contemporary music festival
articles.description: The 49th edition of the new music festival begins this weekend. Where else can you indulge in a world of pure imagination, see the future – and chat over a curry with some of contemporary music’s biggest names? The Huddersfield contemporary music festival – or hcmf , with contemporary-cool lower-case, as it’s styled – celebrates its 49th edition this month, turning the darkness of late November into a beacon of blazing new-music ambition in West Yorkshire. It’s a festival with an extraordinary history. Nowhere else in the UK could you have bumped into Karlheinz Stockhausen and his entourage in a pub in the late 1980s; nowhere else could you have sat in the audience alongside Björk at the town hall; in no other town might you have stumbled on Pierre Boulez, John Cage, Olivier Messiaen and Yvonne Loriod chatting about the best place to have a curry that night. (Well, maybe I can’t guarantee the dinner discussion but all of the above have visited the festival over the past five decades.) Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
articles.description: A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies “Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement. The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it | Editorial
articles.description: Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded. But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist. Many people are angry about “ two-tier policing ” in Britain, supposedly characterised by disproportionately severe enforcement against white people and leniency towards minorities. There is no evidence to support a systemic bias of that kind. By contrast, the data suggests an imbalance of fair treatment goes the other way. People of colour are underrepresented in the police, disproportionately targeted with stop-and-search policies and, if arrested, likelier to have force used against them. Do you have an opinion on the issues raise

articles.title: Why Palantir’s health tech is not the right fit for the NHS | Letter
articles.description: The US firm’s health data system is based on an insurance model of healthcare, not the patient-centred universal service we have in Britain, says Prof Caroline Mitchell The news that NHS England may have overstated the benefits of Palantir for improving efficiency will surprise few frontline clinicians ( NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools, 12 November ) Too often, global digital policy assumes that software designed for the fragmented, insurance-based US healthcare system can simply be adapted to a universal public service elsewhere. A legitimate concern is that algorithms underpinning AI decision-making may be immature in the NHS context, having been developed primarily for a very different US healthcare system. Continue reading...

articles.title: Blaming Ofsted inspectors for the system is unfair | Letters
articles.description: Inspectors and educators alike have been placed under even greater pressure year after year, says Helen Kenny As national officer for the FDA, the union representing a large number of His Majesty’s Inspectors (HMIs), I read Simon Jenkins’ piece with great interest ( Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve, 13 November ). Jenkins dismisses the work of HMIs as merely a “sniff” of the air and a stroll back to Whitehall, showing a lack of knowledge about their role. HMIs are former school leaders, with a deep knowledge and dedication to educating children and young people. They are as far from the typical civil servant (if there is such a thing) that it is possible to get, and in any case are not based in Whitehall. Jenkins does at least suggest an alternative approach, unlike some who are calling for the abolition of Ofsted, but I really question whether he has thought it through. Parents value the provision of inspection, and most educators agree that assessments are fair – independent YouGov polling showed that 74% of educators believed their most recent inspection was accurate. articles.title: What stops us building the houses Britain needs | Letters
articles.description: Emeritus professor Simon Price , Smart Growth UK’s Jon Reeds and former Labour council leader Steve Siddon respond to a column by John Harris John Harris points out the utter inadequacy of Labour’s housing plans, despite Andy Burnham’s passionate advocacy for new social housing ( Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream?, 15 November ). And everyone agrees that we need many more houses. So what’s holding us back? The problem lies in the fiscal rules. At first sight this is puzzling, as borrowing to invest is explicitly allowed (as opposed to borrowing to cover current expenditure). The explanation is the future debt target. Any capital investment increases public debt, and there is a binding debt-to-GDP ratio at the arbitrary and relatively close forecast horizon. Continue reading...

articles.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
articles.description: Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place ( BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November ). The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies. Continue reading...

Yet the newest addition to the paddock is a man whose quietly spoken, understated thoughtfulness and insight are compelling. articles.title: Madden review – Nicolas Cage is a cartoonish NFL legend in David O Russell’s stinker
articles.description: Oscar-nominated director delivers a thoroughly unserious biopic, wasting Christian Bale and Sienna Miller’s talents John Madden was a beloved American original, the burly football coach who segued easily from Super Bowl burnout to television darling to the last name in gaming as the NFL was overtaking baseball as the national pastime. When he wasn’t crashing into family rooms on football Sundays and Thanksgivings to break down the game’s rough complexities into fun-sized morsels, he was pressing flesh with everyday Americans while barnstorming the country in his Madden cruiser – the coach bus he depended on to compensate for his well-documented fear of flying. That the Madden video game franchise outlived the avuncular Minnesotan , whose death at age 85 in 2021 was mourned throughout the sport, is as much a testament to his singular knack for teaching the game’s fundaments as it is to his willingness to bring his classroom to students, wherever they might huddle. But Madden, a new Amazon biopic that can’t decide whether it’s serious or slapstick, has drawn all the wrong lessons. Continue reading...

articles.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
articles.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green mo

articles.title: Theodore Zeldin obituary
articles.description: Revered historian, author and francophile with a novelistic approach to his subject On the website the Oxford Muse , which the francophile Oxford historian Theodore Zeldin set up in 2001 to bring strangers together for mutually liberating conversations, there is a little section on dancing. “Few realise,” he wrote, “how important a part dancing has played in the history of freedom.” During the French Revolution, 700 dance halls opened; in the 1830s, socialists liked dancing the galop because it involved changing partners; in 1968 (or thereabouts) women stopped letting men take the lead. “Dancing is like a carnival, freeing you from what you normally are,” Zeldin wrote. “Dancing together creates harmonies between people with different tastes. That is also what conversation seeks.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Am I Caribbean, or am I a tourist? How art helped me find the answer
articles.description: During my visit to the Fuze Caribbean art fair in the Bahamas, I marvelled at how creators captured the complex nature of Caribbeanness Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here When I tell people I’m travelling to the Bahamas to report on Fuze Caribbean art fair, no one believes I’m really going for work. There are smirks and jokes about it being a tough life, about drinking from coconuts on the beach. The tourist gaze pervades global perceptions of the Caribbean. This week, I speak to the region’s artists about how they use images to speak back. I have Antiguan and Jamaican heritage, so I’m familiar with the fantasies the Caribbean sparks, which Antiguan-American writer Jamaica Kincaid described as so beautiful that its fluffy white clouds, blue spectral waters and “bottomless” black nights seemed “unreal”. Images have done much to flatten the Caribbean in the global imagination – so why shouldn’t Caribbean people use images to speak back? Continue reading...

articles.title: Guarding Stars review – Leighton Meester is a delight in fizzy Netflix holiday romance
articles.description: As a female bodyguard protecting an A-list star, the Gossip Girl actor shines in Christmas movie a cut above the competition Though it is my personal opinion that Christmas should not begin until after Thanksgiving, I am pleased to say that we already have at least one treat in Netflix’s holiday movie assembly line: Guarding Stars, starring Leighton Meester as a frosty bodyguard tasked with protecting Jared Padalecki’s movie star at, of all places, his family’s Montana ranch, falls on the fizzy side of seasonal fluff. Good holiday movies are an exercise in knowing silliness, and so it is a relief when the first 10 minutes of this movie, directed by Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum, strikes the rare December balance between hearth-like warmth (the twinkle in Meester’s chocolate eyes when her Hannah Brooks lands a verbal punch) and complete lunacy (she lands that punch in an argument with her ex about … cuddling … literally seconds after thwarting an assassination attempt in Times Square). As a homespun band of hot would-be cowboys later drawl at a Christmas parade in “Montana” (Canada, per usual): “Christmas is back, y’all.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Apec summit live: Xi, Trump and Putin set to hold historic trilateral in China
articles.description: Leaders of the US, China and Russia to take part in their first trilateral, with developments on trade, AI and global conflicts closely watched Xi Jinping rallies against protectionism as he welcomes Trump to Apec summit What is Apec? Explained in 30 seconds Here’s the Guardian’s Rebecca Bailey on Xi Jinping’s speech today, in which she writes that he reiterated themes of openness and innovation emphasised throughout the summit. “China is an advocate, promoter and forerunner of Asia-Pacific economic cooperation,” he said. He announced China would give US$20 million in funding “to support APEC’s practical cooperation”, and would establish a Apec-focused research centre in Shenzhen. Members of Apec are like passengers riding the same ship. To navigate the waves of the Pacific, we must unite as one and look out for each other. Continue reading...

articles.title: Mike Lynch’s superyacht had unidentified vulnerability to high winds, report finds
articles.description: Bayesian, which sank off Sicily killing seven including tech tycoon, had not been fully assessed, say investigators The superyacht Bayesian, which sank in a storm off Sicily killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter, was vulnerable to knockdown but crew were not aware as it had never been assessed at anchor with its sails down, the final report from the UK’s Marine Accident Investigations Branch (MAIB) has said. The 56-metre (184ft) vessel was anchored near the fishing port of Porticello when it sank during a violent storm shortly before dawn on 19 August 2024. Continue reading...

articles.description: First incursion across boundary since ceasefire deal comes as Eisenkot seeks to form government without Netanyahu The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents. Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road , Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities. articles.title: Anthropic sets share price at $83 for stock market debut, above expected range
articles.description: Artificial intelligence firm positioned for one of the biggest IPOs in history, with trading slated to begin Thursday Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange. The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on Wall Street in June with the biggest market offering ever at $1.77tn. With Anthropic setting its share price at $83, it could now surpass SpaceX. Continue reading...

articles.title: Vincent van Gogh painting auctioned for record $190.4m after dispute over Nazi era sale
articles.description: Chataigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom), which was painted in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, set a new record for the Dutch post-impressionist A Vincent van Gogh masterpiece sold for a record-breaking $190.4m (£144.9m, A$285m) on Wednesday after a dispute between the seller and the heirs of a previous Jewish owner who sold it in the Nazi era, Sotheby’s said. articles.title: Manchester United’s infamous 1974 relegation is a warning from history
articles.description: It may have been a different era, but the 1970s contain salutary lessons for a club in serious decline once again In many ways, there are striking parallels between the Manchester United relegated in 1974 and the Manchester United sitting in the relegation zone at this stage of the season for the first time in 40 years. A legendary manager leaves, his shadow remains; with boardroom dithering and uncertainty, his replacements churn and burn as the club slide over several years. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. Once the lane closure is removed, works will move into the adjacent verge to complete the final phase of w

articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.title: Average 20Y Auction Prices On The Screws
articles.description: Average 20Y Auction Prices On The Screws Unlike last week's debacle of a Treasury auction week, which saw some real stinkers including a catastrophic 10Y auction, moments ago the Treasury sold $42BN in 20Y paper in a perfectly average auction.  The week's lone coupon auction priced at a high yield of 5.459%, down 1bp from October's 5.469% and on the screws with the When Issued. The bid to cover was 2.63, down from 2.73 but right on top of the six-auction average which was also 2.63. The internals were solid, with Indirects rising to tp 60.185% from 58.156%, and the highest since August, if below the 6-auction average of 63.6%. And with Directs taking 26.7%, also in line with the recent average of 24.3%, Dealers were left holding 13.1%, a perfectly average number and just 1% above the recent average of 12.0%. Overall, this was a perfectly average (and forgettable) 20Y auction, although with yields sliding to session lows as the 10Y trades down to a yield of 5.05%, that is hardly bad news in a market that remains extremely on edge.  Tyler Durden Wed, 11/18/2026 - 13:23

articles.description: A Heated Hold: FOMC Minutes To Show The Hawks Were Closer To Winning Than The 10-2 Vote Suggested At 2pm today the Fed releases the minutes of the October 27-28 FOMC meeting, and if there is one thing everyone agrees on it's that they won't matter very much. Recall that three weeks ago the Fed held rates at 3.75%-4.00% in a 10-2 vote , with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissenting in favor of an immediate 25bp hike. It was Cook's first dissent since joining the board in 2022 and, per Fortune, the first time a governor and a regional Fed president dissented on the same side since October 1992 . The statement also upgraded the economy to "strong" from "solid" and promised that the "accumulation of more information" would guide the next move. Translation: we're hiking in December, we just didn't want to do it a week before the midterms (a point several strategists made out loud at the time). Or, as we put it the day after, the hawks lost a vote rather than an argument . articles.description: Pentagon Flunks Financial Audit For Ninth Straight Year Authored by AG News Staff via American Greatness , The Pentagon has failed its financial audit for the ninth fiscal year in a row , the Department of War's Office of Inspector General announced Monday , citing outdated and inadequate financial management systems. The agency-wide audit examined more than $4.8 trillion in assets. About 1,500 auditors from the inspector general's office and independent public accounting firms took part in the review. Investigators found that while the department reported fewer material weaknesses in fiscal 2026, those numbers did not reflect real fixes. Brett Mansfield, the Defense Department's deputy inspector general for audit, said "that reduction stems from consolidation, not resolution." The inspector general's point was that problems had been grouped together, not solved. The inspector general said the components that produce audit reports either kept or improved their opinions in fiscal 2026. Several individual audits remain underway. articles.description: "We Dodged A Bomb": Ex-Con Trainee Indicted Over Device That Emptied 2,500 Homes Around Illinois Ethanol Plant A federal grand jury has indicted a 41-year-old trainee at the Peoria, Illinois, ethanol plant where a bomb was found last Friday , charging him with emailing the company a threat that explosive devices had been placed there. Andrew Kozak of Chillicothe pleaded not guilty to both counts on Tuesday. The threat reached BioUrja Renewables on Friday, Nov. 13, and police found a package at the plant that afternoon. Bomb technicians had it rendered safe by 9:12 p.m., and Police Chief Brad Dixon stressed that it was not a hoax. Peoria police ordered everyone within a mile of the plant to evacuate , including parts of downtown Peoria and East Peoria. Dixon said the order displaced people from an estimated 2,500 homes , and it stayed in place for 18 hours . The FBI has since taken over the case and confirmed the device was a real explosive. The indictment charges Kozak with threats regarding explosives, for threatening to damage and destroy the plant by fire and an explosive, and with interstate communication of a threat. articles.title: Small Vessel Trade Thrives in Hormuz As Iran Targets Supertankers
articles.description: Small Vessel Trade Thrives in Hormuz As Iran Targets Supertankers By Tsvetana Paraskova of OilPrice.com Smaller oil tankers moved in October the most volumes of crude oil out of the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, as Iran targets supertankers and incidents with naval mines and unknown projectiles hit a wartime high. The smaller tankers, which can carry less than half the volumes of a supertanker, shipped 2 million barrels per day (bpd) out of the Strait of Hormuz in October, the highest daily volumes since the war began in February, according to Vortexa data cited by Bloomberg . The shipments on Suezmaxes and Aframaxes, mostly via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, started to materially pick up in September, which coincided with the estimates that overall crude oil flows via the Strait of Hormuz have rebounded and nearly reached pre-war levels. Gulf producers and oil importers have had to continuously adapt to the changing security and shipping conditions in and around the Strait of Hormuz. articles.title: Josephine review – Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan ballast knotty drama about a child witness to a rape
articles.description: Mason Reeves steals the show as an eight year old who stumbles across a sex assault but, despite strong performances, parts of the film feel contrived Beth de Araújo’s new movie takes a very big swing, and it has won prizes and acclaim since its premiere at Sundance. I was unsure about some of the film’s high-concept ideas but the lead performance from its eight-year-old newcomer Mason Reeves is outstanding. Those concerned about spoilers had better look away. Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan play Damien and Claire, a smart professional couple in San Francisco with a bright young daughter called Josephine, marvellously played by Reeves. Damien takes Josephine to Golden Gate Park one morning to play football (they turn out to enjoy watching the English Premier League on TV). She mischievously runs on ahead of her dad to a secluded spot in the park where Damien can’t immediately find her and it is there that Josephine witnesses a rape – not less horrifying for being filmed in long shot. Continue reading...

The so-called teapots have for years enjoyed discounted Iranian and Russian crude, but this year, the war between the United States, Israel, and Iran upended supply chains; the U.S. blockade paralyzed Iranian oil exports and Russian crude became more expensive . "Iraqi crude has emerged as a winner during this period," Liao Na, founder of energy research firm GL Consulting, told Bloomberg. "This could entice other Persian Gulf suppliers to follow suit. articles.description: Bibi Loses The Gavel As Arab Votes Hand Eisenkot Control Of The Knesset Benjamin Netanyahu's camp lost its hold on Israel's parliament on Tuesday night, when the Knesset voted 66-52 to make Yashar's Matan Kahana speaker, ousting Likud's Amir Ohana after a filibuster of more than six hours by the outgoing coalition failed to stop the vote . Kahana won on the votes of the Arab-majority parties. Without Ra'am and the Joint List, which hold 19 seats, the four parties of Gadi Eisenkot's bloc had 48 votes, four fewer than the 52 that went to Likud's candidate, coalition whip Ofir Katz. Only Ra'am's Yasser Hujeirat missed the vote on Kahana's side; Katz took 52 of the Netanyahu bloc's 53 votes, with Likud's Nir Barkat absent. Eisenkot called the result a "proper democratic move which reflects the absolute majority who voted for change." Likud called it "a low point in the history of the Knesset" and said Kahana had been elected with the votes of "terror supporters." Members of Netanyahu's bloc shouted "shame" at each Arab lawmaker who voted for Kahana, according to CNN . The Middle East crisis and the spiking oil and gas prices have shifted the Asian nations' priorities to energy security and generating electricity with homegrown resources. Renewable energy capacity is soaring, not only in the top emerging markets China and India, but also across Southeast Asia, as the Strait of Hormuz crisis hiked LNG prices and dented gas demand. Another clean energy source, nuclear capacity, is also gaining momentum globally. articles.title: The Limits Of Control: Why Human Nature Will Defeat China's AI Socialism
articles.description: The Limits Of Control: Why Human Nature Will Defeat China's AI Socialism Authored by Stu Cvrk via The Epoch Times , Beijing is betting that artificial intelligence (AI) can do what Gosplan never could : see everything, predict everything, and steer 1.4 billion people without the information failures that sank Soviet planning. The bet will probably make the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) better at control than any regime before it. But it will not make socialism work. The flaw in every planned society was never a shortage of data. It was human nature: people lie to those who watch them, officials protect themselves, and nobody can be ordered to care. AI does not cure those problems. It inherits them, scales them, and hides them behind a dashboard. The Machine in Brief The control apparatus already in place is vast. Some 600 million to 700 million cameras feed municipal "city brain" platforms that use face and gait recognition and flag crowds. Grid workers and volunteer informants watch neighborhoods of a few hundred households each. Blacklists bar "untrustworthy" people from planes, trains, and loans. Contrary to Western myth, though, there is still no single national personal score.

Following operational activity, the level of chlorine in the water supply may be boosted temporarily. articles.title: Tanuki: Pon’s Summer review – an adorable raccoon mends the world, one parcel at a time
articles.description: Nintendo Switch/2, PlayStation 4/5, Xbox One/series X/S, PC; Denkiworks/Inpleron Limited This gentle game of fixing and fetching, in which you play as a furry post office worker on a BMX, has a slow, calming magic that delights in routine and restoration Arriving alongside November’s blue wave , Tanuki: Pon’s Summer is a game of quiet restoration that feels perfectly suited to the current moment. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country , except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. Even so, the mixture of steady progress and general low stakes proves intoxicating. This is a short game, but it’s hard not to linger over it. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Like many men of his generation, he tends to push his feelings down from his heart to his toes’: Meera Sodha on her father’s homecoming
articles.description: After a childhood of grief, hardship and hunger, the Guardian food writer’s father Raj always resisted going back to Uganda. What happened when he finally agreed to accompany her on a bittersweet journey into the past? The moment I step off the plane and on to the soil of Entebbe it hits me. Uganda is in my blood. This country that had once existed only in my imagination is finally real. The heat is heavy, the earth bright and rich like dark terracotta. I want to capture this moment – me with my 75-year-old dad, back where he was born. A place he never imagined he would return to. I whoop and reach for my camera, turn it towards my father’s face. “You’re back!” I say. Continue reading...

articles.title: The 14 best men’s boots for winter, from chelseas and lace-ups to wellies
articles.description: Whether you want minimalist or heritage, waterproof or suede, our menswear expert has rounded up the most stylish pairs for every occasion and outfit • The best men’s coats for autumn and winter I haven’t always worn boots. For years I wrote them off – at 5ft 8in, I was convinced anything above the ankle would make my legs look shorter. Then I started wearing them with the right trousers – a straight leg that falls over the top – and realised I’d spent a decade getting winter wrong. All anyone sees is a smart pair of shoes that happens to keep your ankles warm. Here’s the thing: boots needn’t be intimidating. They’re just the wintry version of the leather shoes you already own. A chelsea is your loafer – it goes with pretty much everything in your wardrobe and every event in your diary, Christmas parties included. A derby boot is laced up, a bit sturdier and just as happy with jeans. The chukka is your weekend trainer. And the chunky, rubber-soled ones? Just think of them as an umbrella for your feet. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘You unpack once’: despite reports of ‘poop cruises’ and murder, cruise ships are more popular than ever
articles.description: High-profile crimes and disease outbreaks obscure the fact that the big ships are largely safe – and seeing record numbers of bookings This month, there has been a swell of stories about things going wrong on cruises. A man was arrested in Texas after he allegedly killed a woman during a voyage through the Caribbean. A pianist on a Royal Caribbean cruise from California was rescued by two fishers in the Pacific Ocean after he went overboard. And Singapore seized the MV Odyssey, a US-operated cruise ship that was supposed to offer retirees a “permanent” life at sea. The operator ran out of money because of increased fuel prices and dropped all its passengers off in Cambodia. Continue reading...

articles.title: Lanre Bakare and Carys Afoko are your new culture guides: best podcasts of the week
articles.description: The Guardian’s new twice-weekly show unpicks all the biggest cultural moments. Plus, what is it like to grow up as a YouTube kidfluencer? Is SNL UK funnier than the original? Does it matter if a pop star can sing? The Guardian’s Lanre Bakare and Carys Afoko host this twice-weekly culture videocast . On Thursdays, they zoom in on a big cultural moment with fresh takes. On Sundays, they have a culture swap: introducing each other to a TV series, book, film, album, play or podcast with which they’re obsessed. Hollie Richardson Widely available, episodes twice-weekly from Thursday 19 November Continue reading...

articles.title: DWP glitch threatens my partner’s leave to remain
articles.description: Government department admits it is making a mistake that affects his immigration status but says it can’t put it right The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) is knowingly paying me too much local housing allowance because of a system glitch and it could have serious implications for my partner’s immigration status. I am entitled to shared accommodation allowance as I am under 35 and claim universal credit. However, the DWP is paying me the higher one-bedroom rate for couples. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tell us: have you been misdiagnosed with a medical condition?
articles.description: We are looking for people to share their stories of misdiagnosis, how they realised this had happened, and perhaps found another diagnosis Last month the actor Christina Applegate revealed that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis . She announced that she had the condition in 2021, and has spoken candidly about her experiences of it, becoming a prominent advocate for people living with MS. “I’m back at square one ... I don’t know what’s going on with me.” Applegate said on her podcast MeSsy, adding: “There’s a pretty damn high number of misdiagnoses with MS.” Continue reading...

articles.title: From pyjama parades to blind biscuit taste tests: how we made our ultimate festive gift guide
articles.description: We spent months putting hundreds of presents to the test – here is how we whittled them down • The best Christmas gifts for 2026 If you struggle with the idea of Christmas creep – when the festive season appears to start earlier every year – spare a thought for the team here at Filter HQ. We’ve been in Christmas mode since we packed away last year’s decorations, testing hundreds of presents for our magnum opus: the big 2026 Christmas gift guide . All 369 (we did say it was big) gifts on this year’s list were put through their paces by a crack team of testers covering all ages and tastes. Fashion writer and stylist Sam Deaman – who tested men’s accessories and nightwear – says his partner got fed up with him parading “yet another” pair of pyjamas around their bedroom each night: “It was like Stars in Their Eyes for Christmas gifts,” he says. “‘Tonight, Matthew, I’m going to be … Ebenezer Scrooge!’” Continue reading...

articles.title: The one change that worked: I was burnt out and lonely – until I started ice skating
articles.description: I was stressed and newly diagnosed with ADHD when I decided to choose a new hobby. It awakened my playfulness and immediately improved my quality of life In 2024, I decided to return to England after four and a half years in Lisbon. My first winter back in the UK was psychologically challenging. Working alone on my next book didn’t feel as enjoyable in cold, grey London as it had abroad. The 10th anniversary of my father’s death was approaching and I felt a profound loneliness which, much like the cold, began to seep into my bones. I was struggling, too, to readjust to London’s cost and pace of living. During this time, I was diagnosed with combined-type attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). I used to think I was depressed, but my diagnosis made me realise that part of how I felt was burnout – my brain’s ability to regulate stress was depleted. I felt overwhelmed and would shut down, which would lead to cycles of anxiety, depression and self-criticism. Continue reading...

articles.title: The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings
articles.description: If you discard the peels, skins, stalks and seeds when consuming fruit and vegetables you are missing out on a lot of value. Here’s what to incorporate into your diet – and what to avoid Do you peel your potatoes, deseed your squash and core your cauliflower? A study by King’s College London , published last month in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition , found that people who routinely discard peels, skins, stalks and seeds when preparing fruit and vegetables are missing out on a valuable source of dietary fibre. Ten out of the 12 types of produce the researchers analysed had higher levels of fibre in the scraps than in the flesh. Eating these often overlooked parts could help address the global dietary fibre deficit and tackle food waste, they say. Here, experts share their advice on how to cook and eat “root to tip”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Would more hands-on dads create a more peaceful world? This pioneering scientist thinks so
articles.description: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy unpicked Darwinian sexism to rewrite the story of evolution. Now, she’s turned her attention to the nature of fatherhood ‘Spit here, dear,” Sarah Blaffer Hrdy said to her husband, Dan, handing him a vial when he arrived in New York after the birth of the couple’s first grandchild. It was 2014 and Hrdy was conducting an experiment. Having recorded a 63% jump in oxytocin in her saliva after spending hours cuddling the baby, she wanted to find out if something similar would happen to his hormones. It did, although it took a day longer. In her latest book, Father Time: A Natural History of Men and Babies , Hrdy records with justified pride that “this was the first time anyone had demonstrated a bump in oxytocin levels among doting grandparents”. Continue reading...

Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. articles.title: ‘They learn the job doing the job’: the project helping UK’s Neets into work
articles.description: Labour’s plan to get young unemployed people into work involves overhaul of welfare support, but for those with disabilities, specialist help is crucial When Rory Bowman finished school he joined the cohort of almost a million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – around the country. The 21-year-old has autism and said he was exhausted after struggling for support in mainstream education for years. He didn’t think he could manage university, but couldn’t find a job or training that would accommodate his neurodivergence. Continue reading...

articles.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
articles.description: The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over. Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans. The Guardian’s year in review 2026. On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of the Gu

articles.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
articles.description: Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the  $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year. “The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis , ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they exp

articles.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
articles.description: This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate. Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work , he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here . Continue reading...

articles.title: Sleep paralysis: when you’re awake, but can’t move – or even breathe | Letters
articles.description: Readers recount their terrifying experiences of sleep paralysis in response to an article by Amy Fleming I experienced sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations from childhood and into adulthood, with the episodes only waning in my 30s ( Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis, 11 November ). I never spoke about them to anyone. I experienced hallucinations in the form of severe perspective distortion (oversized bed and rooms) and full hallucinations/dream states, auditory hallucinations (screaming and loud thumping) and, of course, paralysis. I didn’t know at what point I was asleep or if I had woken and could easily slip back into a hypnagogic state. I only became aware of this state as an adult, having been referred to a psychiatrist on an unrelated matter. Continue reading...

articles.title: Have yourself a stress-free Christmas | Letters
articles.description: Tara Padfield will be buying her marmalade and leaving the trees in the woods; Jen Arnall-Culliford says cooking in advance is key. Plus a letter from Alan Ravenscroft I read Ammar Kalia’s article ( Christmas is all in the preparation! Chefs on eight easy things to do now – so you can relax on the big day, 12 November ) with a mixture of disbelief and mounting despair. Apparently, the secret to a stress-free Christmas involves roasting a kilogram of chicken wings and simmering stock for hours, making marmalade from scratch, infusing gin with Sichuan peppercorns and, should we have a spare afternoon, heading into the woods to forage for Douglas fir needles. I had naively imagined that time-saving tips might actually save time. Continue reading...

articles.title: Durham city would be a canny place for parliament | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to a letter suggesting that location scouts for a new site look beyond Manchester, Liverpool and Birmingham Maggie Hamilton is right ( Letters, 12 November ): parliament should move to the north-east of England. The city of the Prince Bishops, Durham, would be an ideal choice. We already have a ready-made and renovated “pitman’s parliament” debating chamber and offices in the historic Redhills building of the Durham Miners’ Association. This is only a five-minute walk from the railway station, which has hourly trains to all points south, including nearby Darlington with its “Treasury North” office, so very convenient. Just around the corner is a brand new, massive and unoccupied riverside office block, apartment and hotel complex. Ideal for business and overnight stays when in session. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ray Bradbury’s warning against mushroom-growing | Brief letters
articles.description: Grow kits | Cat’s humans | Stink bombs | Fascinating facts | Crossword clues Re your report ( Mushroom lovers in UK told to avoid grow kits owing to invasive species risk, 16 November ), anyone contemplating mushroom grow kits should read Ray Bradbury’s 1962 short story Boys! Raise Giant Mushrooms in Your Cellar! If it doesn’t send you screaming out of the house, it’ll certainly put you off growing, or eating, mushrooms. Lynne Scrimshaw London • It is possible to own a dog, but not to be “a cat owner” ( Pass notes, 16 November ); a cat will simply move somewhere else if it chooses. Putting its food in an inaccessible transparent box will certainly accelerate it relocating to where the humans are more compliant. Caroline Westgate Hexham, Northumberland Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘How can we make it riskier?’: the trans theatre troupe turning Virginia Woolf’s Orlando into a ‘porno-biography’
articles.description: A radical new take on the modernist classic includes a Berlin ketamine binge, a ‘goon cave’ and an all-trans cast. The manifesto? To ‘desecrate’ expectations As Orlando’s on a comedown after a ket-heavy night out in Berlin, surrounded by a group of sharp-tongued trans sex workers, Charli Cowgill and Laurie Ward pause the read-through. The scene is new and “it’s feeling a little safe,” Ward says, drumming the table. “How can we make it riskier?” Cowgill and Ward are piss/CARNATION, a theatre-making duo creating fearless, messy and intellectually rigorous work. Audience spit was collected and thrown in their first production, 52 Monologues for Young Transsexuals , a show that collated trans women’s experiences of men and sex work. Ugly Sisters, the pair’s riotous follow-up, relived a brief encounter between a trans woman and Germaine Greer who wrote a caustic article about it. “As a company,” Ward says, “we tend more towards brutal than twee.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Call my (estate) agent! Why celebrities are always buying each other’s homes
articles.description: If you’re seeking a discreet mansion with secluded grounds and plenty of room for your own memorabilia, you may want to remember Joe Pesci’s mistakes before trying the open market Last year, Austin Butler bought a mansion from Brad Pitt. The month before, Brad Pitt bought a mansion from one of the Killers. In 2022, Adele bought Sylvester Stallone’s old house, but only if he let her keep his Rocky statue. Aaron Paul recently sold a house that he bought from The Big Bang Theory’s Jim Parsons, who bought it from Robert Pattinson, after it was previously owned by Noah Wyle, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Tim Curry and the guy who directed Legally Blonde. If this makes it sound to you as if there are only a handful of celebrity-friendly homes on earth, and celebrities spend their lives swapping them around among themselves, then you’re right. Continue reading...

articles.title: Send us your questions for Martin Freeman
articles.description: Do you have something you’d like to ask the man who’s been Sherlock’s right-hand man, a beloved hobbit and the voice of Gromit? Now is your chance When he first charmed audiences in 2001 as phenomenally relatable everyman Tim in a lo-fi BBC mockumentary about office workers, he did so as a hugely loved supporting character. It wasn’t a given that he’d go on to be one of Britain’s most beloved actors, with a role in the highest grossing movie franchise ever, multiple Emmy wins and end up outshining everyone else who shared the screen with him. Yet, in the decades since, that’s just what’s happened: Martin Freeman has starred in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, won one of his two Baftas for being the Dr Watson to Benedict Cumberbatch’s Sherlock Holmes and somehow become a cornerstone of Christmas, with roles in Richard Curtis’s Love Actually and Nativity. Continue reading...

articles.title: Apec summit live: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’
articles.description: Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit What is Apec? Explained in 30 seconds Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday. It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse. Continue reading...

That of course, depends on who ends up as the next resident of the White House, but Newsom made big promises regardless, as the head of California – the world’s fourth largest economy. It began as a fishing trip with his brother, deep within the Sundarbans, a vast landscape of mangrove forest, rivers and islands stretching across the tidal delta of Bangladesh and India. “We went to the riverbank to cut firewood for cooking,” he says. “I was standing there holding the boat in place, while looking towards the bank.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Macron banned smartphones in schools. A month later, France was ablaze. Could they be connected? | Joseph de Weck
articles.description: French teachers argue that a digital detox woke students up to the decrepit state of their schools – and drove them out into the streets Remember the 1999 blockbuster The Matrix ? It may be more than a quarter of a century old, but it has become a byword and a meme for a frighteningly plausible kind of 21st-century tech dystopia. A quick recap: the computer hacker Neo discovers that machines rule over humanity. They keep people trapped in pods, their minds immersed in a virtual reality designed to keep them docile (the “Matrix” of the title). Once he becomes aware of the world he actually inhabits, Neo decides to take up arms. Continue reading...

articles.title: Child doping isn’t just cheating – it’s a global epidemic of abuse and exploitation | Sean Ingle
articles.description: Surveys estimate 10 million minors globally use banned performance-enhancing drugs but suppliers are rarely brought to justice Of all the many stories in Doping Top Secret: Children, a powerful new documentary from the German investigative team that helped expose massive Russian cheating in sport over a decade ago, one keeps replaying in my mind. It involves an East German champion, who breaks his silence half a century on from his Olympic triumph to reveal how being pumped full of anabolic steroids at a young age accelerated his sexual development and, he believes, dramatically altered his behaviour and those of his teammates. “The system abused me as a young person for the good of the state,” says Hans-Georg Aschenbach, who won ski-jump gold in Innsbruck in 1976. Although nothing can prepare you for what he says about how the drugs affected his libido, and particularly what he would sometimes do before he jumped off a large ramp. Continue reading...

articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe | Rafael Behr
articles.description: In a world carved into continental blocs by authoritarians, Britain has to make common cause with its neighbours In the chronicles of 21st-century diplomacy few statements have caused as much offence with as few words as Barack Obama’s 2014 description of Russia as a “regional power” . Vladimir Putin’s politics were defined then, as now, by vengeful resentment of his country’s relegation from superpower status after the cold war. His worldview is warped by a paranoid conviction that Nato never stopped striving to deepen that humiliation, even after the USSR had unravelled. From his Kremlin throne, the Russian president expects to be treated as a colossus of world history. It is hard to overstate how bitterly he hated being dismissed by Obama as a geopolitical B-lister. Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds. Sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons. articles.title: Overlap, underlap or sit back? How Premier League teams use their full-backs
articles.description: The role of full-back has changed massively in recent years. We analyse how all 20 sides are approaching the position By Opta Analyst Overlapping. Underlapping. Inverted. Traditional. The role of full-back has evolved dramatically. Once a defensive-first position that provided some auxiliary attacking support, the role has developed into something far more multifaceted. Just ask right-back Ben White, who – with Riccardo Calafiori on the left – has been an important figure in Arsenal’s superb start to the campaign. Talking a few years ago, he said: “Playing full-back the way [Mikel Arteta] wants is completely different to any other manager. And, as Chris Lewis and others point out, there are a couple of other home nations who have had more dramatic swings. But for Maniza*, a teenager from a conservative town in Pakistan who never leaves the house without her hijab, the selfie she took at home put her at very real risk of an “honour” killing. “My family are really strict and I always wore a hijab. My father didn’t want me to stay in school but my mum pushed him. He said if I got into trouble, he would kill me. It wasn’t just words, he meant it,” she says. Continue reading...

articles.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback
articles.description: After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech. Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs. Continue reading...

Under a new process, Florida had designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights group, a domestic terrorist organization. The university’s Arab Students’ Association decided to cancel the event, and Soboh, who is Palestinian American, was disheartened. “Our existence itself is political,” he said. Continue reading...

articles.title: Fears grow that US will impose sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group. articles.title: Valerie Solanas’s obscenely funny Scum Manifesto is an unignorable burst of female outrage | Emily Woof
articles.description: Before an assassination attempt on Andy Warhol in 1968, Solanas used her fierce writing to confront male supremacy. What can her work teach us about expressing raw anger? It is exhausting to always express anger constructively and reasonably – especially when what you are angry about is violence, exploitation and the inexcusable appetite of disgusting, powerful, greedy men to gain yet more power. Could you please be more balanced in how you express yourself? Could you make your objection to the destruction of the world – through violating not only women but also the planet – well, more constructive? Could you be a little less unpleasant in your anger?
